PREFACE  
The Structure & Liftoff In Combustion Experiment (SLICE) is a precursor to the Coflow 
Laminar Diffusion Flame (CLD Flame) experiment, which is one of the four ACME (Advanced 
Combustion via Microgravity Experiments) investigations that are currently in development for 
conduct within the Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR).  The goal of the experiment is to 
investigate the structure of lifting and lifted flames, where the flame detaches from the nozzle 
and stabilizes at a downstream position.  The results will be used to minimize risk and maximize 
the scientific return of the CLD Flame Experiment.  The SLICE investigation was conducted in 
the Microgravity Science Glovebox (MSG) using the Smoke Point In Coflow Experiment 
(SPICE) hardware.

1.0 
INTRODUCTION 
SLICE, the Structure & Liftoff In Combustion Experiment, is a space station investigation of the 
structure of lifting and lifted flames, where flow conditions and chemistry cause them to detach 
and stabilize downstream of the burner. 
SLICE is a crew-operated combustion experiment that will be conducted within the Microgravity 
Science Glovebox (MSG) on the International Space Station (ISS). A flame of gaseous fuel, such 
as methane which is the primary component of natural gas, will be generated within a small fan-
driven flow duct. With guidance from the ground team, the astronaut will vary the fuel or air 
flow and take still photographs in parallel with video photography. The calibrated still 
photography will enable determination of the soot temperature and volume fraction. 
1.1 
Purpose  
The data will be used to improve modeling capability with the overall goal of increased fuel 
efficiency and reduced pollutant emission in practical combustion devices here on Earth. SLICE 
is a precursor to the Coflow Laminar Diffusion Flame (CLD Flame) experiment which is in 
development for ISS’ Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR) as part of the Advanced Combustion 
via Microgravity Experiments (ACME) project. 
1.2 
Scope  
SLICE is a joint effort of Yale University, the National Center for Space Exploration Research 
(NCSER), NASA, and ZIN Technologies, Inc. The experiment is managed at the NASA Glenn 
Research Center (in Cleveland, OH), which is NASA’s lead for microgravity combustion 
research. If you are looking for more information about SLICE, please visit: 
http://issresearchproject.grc.nasa.gov/MSG/SLICE/

3.0 
SLICE SCIENCE OVERVIEW 
3.1 
Background 
Soot formation in hydrocarbon-fueled flames is an important unresolved problem of combustion 
science that affects the durability and performance of power and propulsion systems, the hazards 
of unwanted fires, the pollutant emissions of combustors and the potential for developing 
computational combustion. 
Coflow laminar diffusion flames are especially valuable for studies of combustion because of the 
availability of accurate numerical modeling with that flame configuration. In particular, excellent 
agreement can be achieved when the flow conditions are such that the flame detaches and lifts 
above (i.e., moves downstream of) the nozzle. A coupled experimental and numerical 
investigation can enable validation and improvements to combustion modeling. Enhanced 
modeling capability is important because it can reduce time and cost in the design of practical 
combustion devices. Furthermore, flame attachment to (or detachment from) a burner or 
condensed-fuel surface is of essential importance in both combustion systems and fire safety. 
The flame attachment point controls the stability of the entire trailing diffusion flame.

3.2 
Objectives 
For diffusion flames of methane, ethylene, and selected nitrogen dilutions of each fuel burning in 
a coflow of air: 
(1) Characterize the structure of the flame, especially its base (i.e., stabilizing region), from 
attached through lifted conditions as a function of the fuel, burner diameter, and flow conditions. 
(2) Identify the liftoff velocity limits as a function of the fuel and burner diameter. 
This will enable refinement of the flame diagnostic settings and test matrix for the CLD Flame 
experiment. It will also allow for a preliminary assessment of the numerical codes’ ability to 
predict the flame structure under the broader conditions that are only found in microgravity 
flames. The computation of attached flames will require modification of the numerical models to 
incorporate burner heat loss. 
3.3

3.3.1 
Fuel Nozzles 
 All nozzles are replaceable on-orbit by the crew 
 Fuel nozzle installed orientation is in the axis of the flow duct 
 Fuel nozzles are circular with a constant internal cross section 
 Off-the-shelf tubes have inner diameter with a tolerance of better than the required ±0.1 
mm  
 The SPICE nozzles available include 0.4, 0.8, ,1.6, 2.1, and 3.2 mm  
 Burner tubes are made of 304 Stainless Steel

Cabin pressure information will be collected from both Columbus and Node 3 using, typically

3.3.5

SLICE testing will be scheduled around planned thruster firing or spacecraft dock or undock. 
The acceleration environment will be measured by SAMS during SLICE testing which will be

3.3.6

 A Nikon D300s camera with a blue-green BG-7 filter that can installed or removed will

There shall be a single ceramic SiC fiber with a diameter of less than 100 microns and shall be

3.4 
Operational Requirments 
The standard test procedure was simplistic in nature.  The flame was ignited, then, the test 
operators relied on voice commands to adjust the fuel flows and air velocity until the flame 
extinguished.   
3.4.1 
Pyrometry Calibration 
The fiber is placed into position in the test chamber and a non-smoking flame is established so 
that the luminous portion of the flame is just below the fiber. Images are then taken with the still 
camera to provide a temperature measurement at the fiber position and an absolute intensity 
calibration.

3.5 
Success Critera 
3.5.1 
Minimum Success 
Still images are acquired for at least 15 different lifted flames with different combinations of fuel 
flow and air velocity with a single fuel, or at least 10 different lifted flames each of two fuels, or 
at least 5 different lifted flames each of 3 or more fuels.   
3.5.2 
High Success 
Still images are acquired of at least 30 different lifted flames total from at least 3 different fuels.  
The still images are acquired with a blackbody characterized camera for soot pyrometry or liftoff 
limits are determined for at least one fuel. 
3.5.3 
Complete Success 
Testing conducted with all 12 fuel bottles, with identification of stability limits and smoke points 
(within the range of the SPICE velocity limits).  Still images are taken of lifted flames with a 
blackbody characterized camera. 
The project would like to acknowledge the efforts of the SLICE Co-Investigator, Dennis Stocker, 
for generating the daily and weekly status updates.  The following sections includes a 
compilation of the status reports that were submitted to the Lead Increment Scientist (LIS) 
during the SLICE science operations conducted in the MSG on ISS.

February 6, 2012 (GMT 037) 
Status Report Originator  
Dennis Stocker, SLICE PS/Co-I 
Science Status

February 9, 2012 (GMT 040) 
Status Report Originator  
Dennis Stocker, SLICE PS/Co-I 
Science Status 
Science operations began today with 100% methane as the fuel.  There 
were 7 flames (i.e., test points) conducted as part of runs 1-2 before the 
fuel bottle was depleted (during the seventh test).  In this testing, data was 
acquired for approximately 35 flow conditions total, which is roughly what 
is expected for a single fuel bottle.  Eleven additional fuel bottles remain. 
Unexpected Events 
We observed significantly greater air flow in the fan calibration today than 
on GMT 037 (i.e., Monday).  Today’s results were very similar to results 
after soot removal during the 2009 SPICE ops which is reassuring, but the 
cause of the different results (i.e., GMT037 vs. 040) is currently not clear.  
Some possible causes include flow blockage on GMT 037, e.g., at or near 
the fan inlet, or “cleaning” resulting from the heat of today’s flames.  The 
SLICE fan calibration is nominally conducted at the end of all SLICE ops 
where we will be alert to future measurements and potential causes for the 
variation.

Science Look Ahead 
Our next ops are with nitrogen-diluted fuel using 70% methane.  A 
major goal of the SLICE research is to extend our modeling 
capability to be able to accurately predict fuel-lean flames.  Before 
the normal flame testing, we’ll be doing a pyromety calibration 
where we’ll be photographing ceramic fiber(s) heated by the flame.  
That reference data combined with the soot pyrometry (via a color 
ratio technique) will allow us to determine the soot volume fraction 
from the still photos. 
Topics for Resolution 
A NCR was generated to identify the problem observed with the 
video overlay.  The NCR is SLICE-NCR-003.  The problem was 
that the video overlay data that is generated by the Video Titler Card 
located in the Video Unit of the Power/Video Unit Assembly 
displayed Hexadecimal data instead of the properly formatted data.  
The video Titler board contains a rechargeable battery that drained 
over the approximately 2 years that it was idle on ISS resulting in 
the Titler settings to reset to their factory default.  The Video Titller 
is capable of being configured to the users desired settings.  The 
crew procedure (MGUEMSGSLCEC001) was developed to allow 
the crew to enter the Titler menu, set the parameters properly, and 
save the settings.  Additonally the SLICE hardware was powered for 
approximately 4 hours to recharge the battery.  The crew procedure 
was successfully performed and even with powering down the 
hardware the settings are maintained.

Don, thanks for your great job in recovering the video overlay data!  It would have been a big loss for 
both ops and science (for SPICE and BASS in addition to SLICE) to have proceeded without that data.  
Testing with the 100% methane went well, where our test matrix is only an estimate of what we might 
accomplish with each bottle.  In the 2 runs, we conducted 7 flames and got data for approx. 35 different 
conditions total - which was about what we had anticipated.  Based on my observations, I (Dennis) 
voiced up more flow conditions for some flames than I had originally intended where that limits the total 
number of flames accomplished.  We look forward to Monday's tests where we will press on to 70% 
methane, beginning with a pyrometry calibration which is needed for determination of the soot volume 
fraction from the still photos.  Meanwhile, we'll take advantage of this week's results to plan how to 
maximize our science return from future tests with the remaining 2 bottles of 100% methane. 
 
Daily Status Reports 
February 13, 2012 (GMT 044) 
Status Report Originator  
Dennis Stocker, SLICE PS/Co-I 
Science Status 
There was a late planning change where today’s testing was conducted 
with 40% methane instead of the 70% methane that had been planned.  
Review of the GMT 040 results made the SLICE PI concerned that 
microgravity-enhanced soot production would degrade the pyrometry 
calibration if the soot accumulated on the ceramic fibers.  Fuel dilution 
diminishes soot production, so the decision was made to begin with the 
most dilute fuel so as to avoid contamination of the silicon carbide (SiC) 
fibers.  Science operations began with the pyrometry calibration to get 
reference images of glowing ceramic fiber(s) – heated by a flame - that will 
allow determination of the soot volume fraction from the still photos of the 
flames.  Two calibration tests were conducted (i.e., test point 49 was 
repeated once) followed by four standard tests (i.e., flames) from run 8 
before the fuel bottle was depleted (during the final test).  Data was 
acquired for approximately 32 flow conditions total (from 6 flames total), 
which is similar to what was accomplished on GMT 040 and roughly what 
is expected for a single fuel bottle.  It must be understood that the number 
of tests (i.e., flames) conducted is very highly dependent on the flow 
conditions voiced up by SLICE.  More conditions than had been planned 
were voiced up today because the 0g flames didn’t lift when anticipated, 
and this diminished the number of tests conducted, i.e., flames ignited.  
Ten additional fuel bottles remain and the SLICE team is reassessing how 
to make the most out of that remaining fuel. 
Unexpected Events 
We are still seeing an inconsistency in the fan calibration, where today’s 
results suggest a significantly lower air flow than on GMT 040 but a little 
more than observed on GMT 037.  The calibration was conducted twice 
today with the glovebox both sealed (nominal) and open, but those two 
conditions gave nearly identical results.  The curves are all very similar in 
shape but offset from one another, where the cause of the variation is not 
yet understood.  It is not known whether the variation is because of 
inconsistencies in the actual flow, the measurement, or both.  The SLICE 
team is working to understand the data.

Don, thanks for your care with the ceramic fibers for the pyrometry calibration of the still photos, where 
that will enable our determination of the soot volume fraction in the flames.  In the testing on GMT 044, 
which was with 40% methane (diluted with nitrogen), a total of 6 tests were conducted, including two 
pyrometry calibrations and 4 standard tests, where the latter included 30 distinct flow conditions 
including several where the flame was lifting and partially detached from the  burner tube.  The 
microgravity flames have been found to be more stable, i.e., resistant to lifting, than anticipated so future 
testing will focus on smaller burner tubes, and thus higher jet velocities.  We’ve seen significant variation 
in the fan calibration curves, which is why we requested multiple fan calibrations on GMT 044 and 048.  
The two fan calibrations that you conducted on GMT 044 were nearly identical, but showed readings that 
were significantly lower than those on GMT 040 and slightly higher than those on GMT 037.  The 
existing curves, including pre-launch (in 2008) and during the 2009 SPICE ops, all exhibit a very similar 
shape but are often offset vertically.  Thus far, we don’t yet understand the cause of the variation, or 
even if the variation is in the flow itself or just the readings.  Next week’s testing includes 20% ethylene 
(diluted with nitrogen) and 100% propane, where the tests are focused on lifting (SLICE) and smoke 
points (SPICE), respectively. 
 
Daily Status Reports 
February 17, 2012 (GMT 048) 
Status Report Originator  
Dennis Stocker, SLICE PS/Co-I 
Science Status 
Today’s activity was conducted with 70% methane (diluted with nitrogen) 
and included two fan calibrations (conducted before and after the regular 
ops), a pyrometry calibration test (including 3 flow conditions) that will be 
used to determine the soot volume fraction from the digital stills, and 8 
standard tests (flames) including approximately 26 flow conditions.  
Through today’s selection of test points and voiced-up flow settings, 
results were acquired for a broader range of conditions than achieved in 
previous sessions.  More importantly, these tests included photography of 
lifted flames, which is the principal experimental objective for SLICE.   
While SLICE is clearly limited on fuel, good use was made of the bottle 
today. 
Unexpected Events 
None.  FYI, the two fan calibrations conducted today were very similar to 
each other, where the post-testing calibration was essentially identical with 
that on GMT 044.  They were also close to the calibration on GMT 037, 
making the calibration on GMT 040, with its significantly higher flows, an 
outlier.  Yet that day’s readings were very similar to those from a post-
cleaning calibration in the 2009 SPICE ops, suggesting the possibility in a 
systematic, but yet unknown, cause for the outliers. 
Science Look Ahead 
Monday’s testing is with 20% ethylene, where that fuel is of interest as a 
contrast to the methane because it is much more highly sooting.  Monday 
will not include a pyrometry calibration, as no more are planned for SLICE, 
but will focus on lifting and lifted flames.

Don, thanks for your efforts and skill in capturing images of the lifted flames.  The microgravity flames 
have lifted at signficantly greater velocities than the normal-gravity flames, but upon lifting have been 
much less stable.  In the testing on GMT 048, which was with 20% ethylene (diluted with nitrogen), a 
total of 8 tests were conducted, including some repeats, with 32 distinct flow conditions including two 
where the flame was detached from the  burner tube.  As of GMT 054, a total of 27 standard tests (i.e., 
flames) were conducted including approximately 120 flow conditions.  The SLICE fan calibrations have 
shown minor day-to-day variation, where the calibration conducted on GMT 040 appears to be an 
outlier, and where the cause for the significantly higher flow readings on that day is unknown.  The 
results from GMT 040 are quite close to those obtained after the soot removal during the 2009 SPICE 
ops (on GMT 166), suggesting the possibility of a systematic cause.  The agreement of the typical 
SLICE results with those from the end of the 2009 SPICE ops seems to support this idea, but both could 
be coincidences.  Recent testing indicates that the higher flow readings from GMT 044 are not the result 
of either (1) the glovebox being open (i.e., where the gloveports are not sealed) or (2) the glovebox air 
circulation being on.  Much higher flow readings are observed when the front door of the SPICE 
experiment assembly is open, although that condition can lead to readings that significantly exceed 
those from GMT 040.  Next week’s testing includes more lifted flame tests with the 100% and 40% 
methane (diluted with nitrogen), but there will be a return to smoke point testing in future weeks.

This week's testing went very well, where we conducted a total of 25 lifting tests (i.e., ignitions), including 
approx. 140 flow conditions.  They were conducted on GMT 058 and 061 with 100% and 40% methane 
(diluted with nitrogen), respectively.  Importantly, the testing on GMT 061 included the right combination 
of factors - including Don's careful flow adjustments - to yield stable lifted flames, which can be simpler 
to numerically model and as such are the preferred flame configuration for this research.  Thanks too to 
Don for his great fisheye photos of the hardware setup within the glovebox.  The fan calibrations for both 
days gave similar results to previous sessions (with the exception of GMT 040), so flow degradation has 
not been an issue.  Next week's tests will include both lifting tests on Monday (GMT 065) and smoke 
point tests on Thursday (GMT 068) with 70% methane and 100% ethane, respectively.  Regarding the 
latter, ethane is the intermediate alkane between methane and propane and was not part of SPICE's 
2009 test matrix.

to longer residence times and enhanced soot production.  SPLICE testing will presumably come to a 
close on Friday (GMT 083) with smoke point tests using 100% ethylene.  However, as a reminder,

comparison when the flames are close to the burner, e.g., less than 1 cm per Co-Investigator Mitch 
Smooke.  And the broad range of conditions in the microgravity flames is helpful in revealing 
shortcomings in existing combustion codes for chemical kinetics, e.g., GRI-Mech.  We also look forward 
to hearing about the progress on our colleagues’ Burning and Suppression of Solids (BASS) experiment.
